newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices ease back after weather-related gains.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices ease back after weather-related gains.

text.p: World oil prices eased back on Tuesday as the market took stock of Monday's healthy weather-related gains, traders and analysts said.
Benchmark Brent crude oil futures, traded at the International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) for delivery in February, were 23 cents a barrel down on the day at $23.66 at 1635 GMT.

World oil inventories are low and the prospect of colder weather in key oil-consuming regions in north America overshadows news of the recent resumption of Iraqi oil exports, keeping prices stubbornly high in the short term.
"The bottom line is -- Mother Nature leads the way for now," said Charles Gray of Prudential-Bache. "Keep an eagle eye on weather forecasts."
Iraq's limited oil-for-food sale agreement with the United Nations came into force on December 10 and allows Iraq to sell $2 billion of oil over the next six months.
Port officials at the Iraqi oil export terminal of Mina al-Bakr said on Tuesday that the first tanker of oil, the 265,000 tonne Leonidas, is now loading and is due to leave on Wednesday.
Iraqi oil is also flowing via pipeline to the Turkish port of Ceyhan.
But traders at the IPE said that the news from Iraq has been factored into prices for now and the market's focus of attention was elsewhere.
"Forecasts for colder weather in the U.S. over then next several days did the work for the bulls on Monday," said London-based Leslie Nicholas of GNI research.

Current U.S. stocks of heating oil -- which exert a strong influence over world oil prices -- are over 12 million barrels, or around 10 percent, below last year's levels, and another cold winter would make it harder to replenish those inventories.

"The cold snap is expected to extend from the north into Texas and meteorologists even talk of disruption to gulf Coast refinery operations... this latter issue has pushed the Iraq issue into the background," Nicholas said.
But he said that while the effect of Iraqi exports would take time to filter through to world prices, "the impact will eventually be felt."
Having been ostracised by world oil markets since its invasion of Kuwait six years ago, Iraq has found little difficulty persuading foreign oil firms to rekindle old trading ties.

Twelve companies have already signed contracts totalling over 350,000 barrels per day with Iraq's state oil marketing organisation SOMO. These include Bayoil and Coastal of the U.S., France's Elf and Total, Japan's Mitsubishi Corp, and Russia's Lukoil.
Negotiations are continuing with a range of companies from Europe, Japan, South America and the United States.
